title: Primitive-function reconstruction for closed subgroups of vector groups
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] of characteristic $p>0$, and put $\sigma(c)=c^p$. Define $A=k_\sigma[F]$ to be the ring of finite sums $\sum_i c_iF^i$, with coefficientwise addition and multiplication $(cF^i)(bF^j)=c\,b^{p^i}F^{i+j}$. For a commutative $k$-algebra $R$, give its additive group the left $A$-module structure $c\cdot x=cx$ and $F\cdot x=x^p$. For a finitely generated left $A$-module $M$ [def-weil-finitely-generated-module], let $U(M)$ be the functor on commutative $k$-algebras with values $U(M)(R)=\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,R)$, with pointwise addition. This functor is represented by an affine commutative $k$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], admitting a closed embedding into some finite power of $\mathbf G_a$ [def-sc-gm-ga, def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. For every affine $k$-group scheme $G$ of finite type admitting such a closed embedding, put $P(G)=\operatorname{Hom}_{k\text{-groups}}(G,\mathbf G_a)$; addition is pointwise, $c\cdot f$ is multiplication of $f$ by $c$, and $F\cdot f$ is the composite of $f$ with $x\mapsto x^p$. Then $P(G)$ is a finitely generated left $A$-module and evaluation gives an isomorphism of $k$-group schemes $G\xrightarrow{\sim}U(P(G))$, whose value on every $R$ sends $g\in G(R)$ to $(f\mapsto f_R(g))$. Here $\mathbf G_a(R)=(R,+)$, and $\operatorname{Hom}_A$ means additive maps respecting the displayed $A$-actions.

source.place: Theorem 14.46, printed p.295, with Proposition 14.41, Remark 14.42, Lemmas 14.43-14.44, printed pp.293-294, and equation (98). The represented functor is the universal U of Proposition 14.41.

proof.text: For an affine group $G=\operatorname{Spec}C$, identify a morphism $f:G\to\mathbf G_a$ with $a=f^*(t)\in C$. By the coordinate Hopf identities and $\Delta(t)=t\otimes1+1\otimes t$, it is a group homomorphism exactly when $\Delta_C(a)=a\otimes1+1\otimes a$. This equation forces $\epsilon_C(a)=0$ and $S_C(a)=-a$ by applying the counit and antipode identities. Thus $P(G)$ is precisely this linear space of primitive elements. Frobenius additivity shows that $a\mapsto a^p$ preserves it and satisfies $F(ca)=c^pF(a)$. The rule $(cF^i)a=ca^{p^i}$ gives the stated left $A$-action, since composition of these operators has the displayed skew multiplication.

For any left $A$-module $V$, not yet assumed finitely generated, put $T(v)=Fv$ and construct $B(V,T)$ and $j$ as in the basis node. The symmetric-algebra universal property followed by the quotient property gives, naturally for every commutative $k$-algebra $R$, a bijection
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{k\text{-alg}}(B(V,T),R)=\{h:V\to R\text{ linear}:h(Tv)=h(v)^p\}=\operatorname{Hom}_A(V,R).$$
Indeed both sides send $j(v)$ to $h(v)$; respecting $k$ and $F$ is exactly respecting every finite sum in $A$. This also proves uniqueness of all algebra maps out of $B(V,T)$ from their values on $j(V)$.

source.place: Proposition 14.41, printed p.293, using the abelian form of the construction on p.207.

proof.text:
Define algebra maps on $B=B(V,T)$ by
$$\Delta(jv)=jv\otimes1+1\otimes jv,\qquad\epsilon(jv)=0,\qquad S(jv)=-jv.$$
They exist by step 2: for $\Delta$ the $p$th-power equation is $(jv\otimes1+1\otimes jv)^p=j(Tv)\otimes1+1\otimes j(Tv)$; the other two equations are immediate, including $p=2$. The tensor-product algebra structure is the cited one. Coassociativity, the two counit identities, the two antipode identities and symmetry of $\Delta$ hold on each $jv$, hence on $B$ by uniqueness in step 2. The Hopf-spectrum functor therefore supplies an affine commutative group $\operatorname{Spec}B$ representing the functor in step 2. The displayed comultiplication induces pointwise addition on $\operatorname{Hom}_A(V,R)$.

source.place: Proposition 14.41 and Remark 14.42, printed pp.293--294; Hopf identities spelled out from the construction.

proof.text: If $M$ has $A$-generators $m_1,\ldots,m_r$, every $j(m)$ is a linear combination of $j(F^im_s)=j(m_s)^{p^i}$. Since $B(M,F)$ is generated by $j(M)$, it is generated as a $k$-algebra by the finite list $j(m_s)$. Hence it is a quotient of $k[t_1,\ldots,t_r]$, and its spectrum is a closed subscheme of $\mathbf G_a^r$. This is a group embedding because each coordinate $j(m_s)$ is primitive. The finite affine polynomial presentation makes its structure morphism finite type directly from the finite-affine-cover definition. This proves all the representability, commutativity, finite-type and embedding assertions for $U(M)$, including $M=0$ and $r=0$.

source.place: Remark 14.42, printed p.294; explicit finite-generation calculation.

proof.text:
Choose a $k$-basis $(e_i)$ of $V$. The basis node gives linearly independent monomials $b_a=\prod j(e_i)^{a_i}$ with $0\le a_i<p$. Multiplicativity of $\Delta$ gives
$$\Delta(b_a)=\sum_{r+s=a}\left(\prod_i\binom{a_i}{r_i}\right)b_r\otimes b_s.$$
For every $a$ with $\sum a_i\ge2$, choose $i$ with $a_i>0$ and split $a=\delta_i+(a-\delta_i)$. Both terms are nonzero, and the coefficient of $b_{\delta_i}\otimes b_{a-\delta_i}$ in a linear combination's reduced coproduct is exactly $a_i$ times its $b_a$ coefficient: no other monomial can contribute to this tensor. Since $1\le a_i<p$, it is nonzero in $k$. Thus every primitive is in $j(V)$; its constant coefficient is zero by the counit. Conversely all $j(v)$ are primitive. Therefore $j$ identifies $V$ with the primitive space of $B(V,T)$. The subspaces spanned by $b_a$ with $\sum a_i\le n$ are exhaustive, start with $k1$, and satisfy the coalgebra filtration condition, by the same formula.

source.place: Lemma 14.43, printed p.294; ordinary monomials instead of divided monomials give the same coefficient test.

proof.text: Let $C$ be a commutative Hopf $k$-algebra and let $V\subseteq C$ be a linear subspace of primitive elements stable under $p$th powers. Step 2 extends the inclusion to an algebra map $q:B(V,F)\to C$. The formulas on generators show that it commutes with comultiplication and counit. If it were not injective, the connected-filtered-coalgebra kernel lemma, applied to the filtration in step 5 with distinguished element $1$, would give a nonzero primitive element in its kernel. Step 5 says this element is $j(v)$, and then $q(j(v))=v$ forces $v=0$, a contradiction to injectivity of $j$. Thus $q$ is injective. Notice that neither $V$ nor $C$ needs a finite-generation assumption here.

source.place: Agent algebraic kernel argument from Lemma 14.43, printed p.294, replacing the quotient-map detour of Lemma 14.44.

proof.text: Now fix a closed group embedding $G\hookrightarrow\mathbf G_a^r$ and write $C=k[G]$. The coordinate map $k[t_1,\ldots,t_r]\twoheadrightarrow C$ is surjective; let $x_s$ be the images of the coordinates. They are primitive by step 1. Let $N$ be their left $A$-span inside $P(G)\subseteq C$. Then $N$ is generated by $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ as an $A$-module. Step 6 makes $q:B(N,F)\to C$ injective; it is also surjective since the $x_s$ generate $C$ as an algebra. This algebra isomorphism respects the Hopf maps, so it identifies their primitive spaces. Step 5 identifies the primitive space of $B(N,F)$ with $N$, and $q$ is the inclusion on $N$. Consequently $P(G)=N$, proving finite generation without presupposing it for the construction of $B(P(G),F)$.

source.place: Theorem 14.46, printed p.295; explicit finite-generation argument using the primitive calculation of Lemma 14.43.

proof.text: Since $P(G)=N$, the isomorphism of step 7 is exactly the map $B(P(G),F)\to C$ sending $j(f)$ to the coordinate function $f$. Taking spectra gives $G\simeq U(P(G))$. For any commutative $k$-algebra $R$, a point $g:C\to R$ is sent to the $A$-linear map $f\mapsto g(f)=f_R(g)$. The formula is natural in $R$, and preserves addition since every $f$ is a group homomorphism. It is therefore the asserted evaluation isomorphism with its specified value on all $R$-points, including nonreduced algebras.

source.place: Theorem 14.46, printed p.295, with the adjunction (98) and its evaluation map.
